Merge sort.** $\Theta(n\log n)$ in every case and stable, at the price of $O(n)$ extra memory; its *merge* is a reusable machine. - **A4. The vocabulary of sorting {#sec-salgo-a0} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Before comparing sorts we need words for what they promise. **Comparison sort**: it learns about the keys only by asking "is $x < y$?". **In place**: it needs only $O(1)$ extra memory (we also accept the $O(\log n)$ recursion stack). **Stable**: two items with equal keys come out in the order they went in. **Adaptive**: it runs faster when the input is already partly sorted. **Inversion**: a pair of positions that is in the wrong order; the number of inversions measures how unsorted an array is. ::: **The comparison model.** A comparison sort may move items around however it likes, but the only way it learns anything about the keys is to compare two of them. We count its cost as the number of comparisons (and sometimes the number of moves). Merge sort, quicksort, heapsort, insertion and selection sort are all comparison sorts; so are Python's `sorted` and C++'s `std::sort`, which accept any type with a `<`. Counting sort is not: it uses a key as an array index. **Inversions.** For an array $a[0..n)$, an inversion is a pair $i < j$ with $a[i] > a[j]$. A sorted array has $0$ inversions; a strictly decreasing one has the maximum, $\binom n2 = n(n-1)/2$. In a random permutation each of the $\binom n2$ pairs is inverted with probability $\tfrac12$, so the expected count is $n(n-1)/4$. Swapping two *adjacent* out-of-order items removes exactly one inversion and creates none, which is why any sort that only swaps neighbours (insertion sort, bubble sort) needs at least as many swaps as there are inversions. **Stability, precisely.** A sort is stable if, whenever positions $i < j$ hold items with equal keys, the item from $i$ is output before the item from $j$. Stability is invisible when you sort plain numbers (equal numbers are indistinguishable) and essential when you sort *records* by one field: it is what lets "sort by name, then stably by grade" produce grade order with names alphabetical inside each grade (@sec-srt-a1). Every sort in this chapter goes through the same harness below. It checks the output against `sorted` on empty, tiny, sorted, reversed, all-equal and random inputs with few or many distinct keys. Then it tests stability with **records** that compare only by key but remember their input position. A sort that claims stability must keep the positions in order on every trial. A sort that does not claim it must be caught out: the harness searches for a concrete **witness**, a small key list on which the sort reorders equal keys. A second helper counts comparisons by wrapping each value in an object whose `<` increments a counter, so every complexity claim below is a measured number, not a slogan. ::: {#arr-salgo-a0-harness .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} class a0_Rec: """A record compared only by its key k; tag remembers its input position.""" __slots__ = ("k", "tag") def __init__(self, k, tag): self.k, self.tag = k, tag def __lt__(self, o): return self.k < o.k def __le__(self, o): return self.k <= o.k def __gt__(self, o): return self.k > o.k def __ge__(self, o): return self.k >= o.k def __eq__(self, o): return self.k == o.k __hash__ = None A0_CMP = [0] # global comparison counter class a0_Cnt: """A value whose every comparison is counted.""" __slots__ = ("v",) def __init__(self, v): self.v = v def __lt__(self, o): A0_CMP[0] += 1; return self.v < o.v def __le__(self, o): A0_CMP[0] += 1; return self.v <= o.v def __gt__(self, o): A0_CMP[0] += 1; return self.v > o.v def __ge__(self, o): A0_CMP[0] += 1; return self.v >= o.v def __eq__(self, o): A0_CMP[0] += 1; return self.v == o.v __hash__ = None def a0_comparisons(sort_fn, values): """Run sort_fn on counted copies of values; check the result; return #comparisons.""" A0_CMP[0] = 0 out = sort_fn([a0_Cnt(v) for v in values]) used = A0_CMP[0] assert [c.v for c in out] == sorted(values) return used def a0_inversions(a): return sum(1 for i in range(len(a)) for j in range(i + 1, len(a)) if a[i] > a[j]) def a0_inputs(trials=200, max_n=40): yield from ([], [7], [2, 1], [1, 1], list(range(30)), list(range(30, 0, -1)), [5] * 20) for _ in range(trials): spread = random.choice([2, 10, 1000]) # few, some, many distinct keys yield [random.randint(-spread, spread) for _ in range(random.randint(0, max_n))] def a0_is_stable_on(sort_fn, keys): recs = [a0_Rec(k, i) for i, k in enumerate(keys)] return [(r.k, r.tag) for r in sort_fn(recs)] == sorted((r.k, r.tag) for r in recs) def a0_check(sort_fn, stable): """Correctness on many inputs; Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix {#sec-salgo-a1} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Walk left to right keeping `a[0..i)` sorted. Take `a[i]`, **shift** every larger element of the prefix one cell right, and drop `a[i]` into the gap. It is how most people sort a hand of cards. The work is one shift per inversion, so it costs $O(n^2)$ on a reversed array but only $O(n)$ on an array that is already nearly sorted, and it is **stable** and **in place**. ::: **How it works.** Hold the next key in your hand, compare it with the sorted prefix from the right, and shift each larger element one step right until you meet an element that is not larger. Put the key in the hole. ```text for i in 1 .. n-1: key = a[i]; j = i - 1 while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: # strict '>' : an equal key is never jumped over a[j+1] = a[j]; j -= 1 # shift right to open a gap a[j+1] = key # drop the key into the gap ``` ::: {#fig-salgo-a1-anim} ::: {#c56ed385 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Watch the shift counts: $1, 1, 0, 4, 3$, nine in all, which is exactly the number of inversions of the input. ::: **Invariant and proof.** *At the start of iteration $i$, the prefix `a[0..i)` holds the original first $i$ elements, in sorted order.* Initially ($i = 1$) the prefix is one element, trivially sorted. During iteration $i$ the while loop moves exactly the prefix elements greater than `key` one cell right, keeping their order, and stops at the first element $\le$ `key` (or at the left end). Placing `key` just after that element leaves `a[0..i+1)` sorted and made of the original first $i+1$ elements, so the invariant holds for $i+1$. When the loop ends, $i = n$ and the whole array is sorted. **Stability** comes from the strict test `a[j] > key`: the scan stops at an equal element, so `key` lands *after* every earlier equal key, never before it. **Cost.** Each shift moves one prefix element past `key`, and that pair was an inversion; no other moves happen. So the number of shifts is *exactly* the number of inversions $I$. Each iteration makes one comparison per shift plus at most one comparison that fails, so the comparisons $C$ satisfy $I \le C \le I + n - 1$. | Input | Comparisons | Shifts | Time | |---|---|---|---| | sorted (best) | $n - 1$ | $0$ | $\Theta(n)$ | | random (average) | $\approx n^2/4$ | $n(n-1)/4$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | | reversed (worst) | $n(n-1)/2$ | $n(n-1)/2$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | Extra space $O(1)$, in place, stable, adaptive ($O(n + I)$), and **online**: it can sort items as they arrive, because it never looks at an item before inserting it. **Binary insertion sort.** The prefix is sorted, so the slot for `key` can be found by binary search with $\lceil \log_2(i+1) \rceil$ comparisons instead of a linear scan. Use `bisect_right` (the slot *after* equal keys) to stay stable. This cuts comparisons to $O(n\log n)$, but the elements still have to move, so the time stays $O(n^2)$ in the worst case. It pays when comparisons are expensive and moves are cheap (a block shift is one `memmove`), which is exactly why Timsort uses it for short runs (@sec-salgo-a8). ::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"} #### Python ::: {#arr-salgo-a1-demo .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} def a1_insertion(a): a = list(a) for i in range(1, len(a)): key, j = a[i], i - 1 while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: # strict '>' keeps equal keys in input order a[j + 1] = a[j] j -= 1 a[j + 1] = key return a def a1_shifts(a): """Same loop, returning the number of shifts instead of the array.""" a, shifts = list(a), 0 for i in range(1, len(a)): key, j = a[i], i - 1 while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: a[j + 1] = a[j]; j -= 1; shifts += 1 a[j + 1] = key return shifts def a1_binary_insertion(a): a = list(a) for i in range(1, len(a)): key = a[i] pos = bisect_right(a, key, 0, i) # slot after all keys <= key: stable a[pos + 1:i + 1] = a[pos:i] # shift the block right by one a[pos] = key return a a0_check(a1_insertion, stable=True) a0_check(a1_binary_insertion, stable=True) for _ in range(200): # shifts == inversions, I <= C <= I + n - 1 a = random.sample(range(100), random.randint(1, 30)) inv, c = a0_inversions(a), a0_comparisons(a1_insertion, a) assert a1_shifts(a) == inv and inv <= c <= inv + len(a) - 1 assert a0_comparisons(a1_insertion, list(range(50))) == 49 # best case n - 1 assert a0_comparisons(a1_insertion, list(range(50, 0, -1))) == 50 * 49 // 2 # worst case for _ in range(100): # binary insertion: sum of ceil(log2(i+1)) comparisons a = [random.randint(0, 99) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 60))] bound = sum(math.ceil(math.log2(i + 1)) for i in range(1, len(a))) assert a0_comparisons(a1_binary_insertion, a) <= bound assert a1_shifts([5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3]) == a0_inversions([5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3]) == 9 print("a1 insertion OK") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a1 insertion OK ``` ::: ::: #### C++ ```cpp #include using namespace std; // Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix. It is also the right tool for data that is known to be nearly sorted (a log with a few late arrivals) and for keeping a small list sorted as items arrive. On a linked list it needs no shifting at all, only relinking (@sec-salgo-p1-b). ## A2. Selection sort: minimise writes, not comparisons {#sec-salgo-a2} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} For each slot $i$, **scan** the unsorted tail for its minimum and **swap** it into slot $i$. It always makes $\binom{n}{2}$ comparisons, whatever the input, but at most $n-1$ swaps. When moving an element is the expensive operation (large records, writes to flash memory), that small write budget is the one to beat. It is **in place** but **not stable**: the swap can carry an element far to the right, past an equal one. ::: **How it works.** The array is split into a sorted prefix and an unsorted tail. Each pass finds the smallest element of the tail with one linear scan and swaps it to the front of the tail, which grows the prefix by one. ```text for i in 0 .. n-2: m = index of the minimum of a[i .. n-1] # one linear scan of the tail swap(a[i], a[m]) # at most one swap per pass ``` ::: {#fig-salgo-a2} ::: {#24c59845 .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](012_sorting_algorithms_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=497 height=489} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](012_sorting_algorithms_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-2.png){width=497 height=489} ::: ::: Selection sort on $[5,2,4,1,3]$. Pass 0 finds the minimum $1$ at index 3 and swaps it to the front; pass 1 finds $2$ already in place. Each pass grows the green prefix by exactly one; the amber cell is where the swapped-out element went. ::: **Invariant and proof.** *Before pass $i$, `a[0..i)` holds the $i$ smallest elements of the input, in sorted order.* It holds for $i = 0$. Pass $i$ swaps the minimum of the tail `a[i..n)` into position $i$; every element of the prefix is $\le$ every tail element (they are the $i$ smallest), so the new prefix `a[0..i+1)` is sorted and holds the $i+1$ smallest. After pass $n-2$ the prefix holds the $n-1$ smallest and the last element is the largest, so the array is sorted. **Cost.** Pass $i$ compares the current minimum with each of the $n - 1 - i$ other tail elements, so the total is $\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}(n-1-i) = \binom n2$ comparisons on *every* input: selection sort is not adaptive. It makes at most one swap per pass, so at most $n - 1$ swaps, $O(n)$ writes. | Input | Comparisons | Swaps | Time | |---|---|---|---| | any | $n(n-1)/2$ | $\le n - 1$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | Extra space $O(1)$, in place, **not stable**, not adaptive. ::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"} #### Python ::: {#arr-salgo-a2-demo .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} def a2_selection(a): a, n = list(a), len(a) for i in range(n - 1): m = i for j in range(i + 1, n): if a[j] < a[m]: # strict '<' keeps the FIRST minimum ... m = j a[i], a[m] = a[m], a[i] # ... but this swap can still break stability return a def a2_swaps(a): a, n, swaps = list(a), len(a), 0 for i in range(n - 1): m = min(range(i, n), key=lambda j: a[j]) if m != i: a[i], a[m] = a[m], a[i]; swaps += 1 return swaps a2_witness = a0_check(a2_selection, stable=False) for n in (0, 1, 2, 10, 37): # exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons on any input for a in (list(range(n)), list(range(n, 0, -1)), random.sample(range(1000), n)): assert a0_comparisons(a2_selection, a) == n * (n - 1) // 2 assert a2_swaps(a) <= max(0, n - 1) # the O(n)-writes promise assert a2_selection([5, 2, 4, 1, 3]) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] print("a2 selection OK; instability witness:", a2_witness) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a2 selection OK; instability witness: [1, 1, 0] ``` ::: ::: #### C++ ```cpp #include using namespace std; // Selection sort: swap the minimum of the unsorted tail into place. Merge sort: divide, conquer, and the reusable merge {#sec-salgo-a3} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Split the array in half, **sort each half recursively**, then **merge** the two sorted halves into one sorted array in a single left-to-right sweep. The recursion is $\log_2 n$ levels deep and each level does $n$ work in total, so the cost is $\Theta(n \log n)$ in *every* case: no lucky pivot, no bad input. The merge takes from the left half on ties, so the sort is **stable**. The price is $O(n)$ extra memory for the merge buffer. ::: Insertion and selection sort both grow a sorted prefix one element at a time, which is why they are quadratic. Merge sort is the first sort here that uses **divide and conquer**: it splits the problem into two half-size problems, solves them independently, and combines the answers cheaply. Quicksort: partition, recurse, and select one rank {#sec-salgo-a4} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Pick a **pivot**. **Partition** the array so that everything smaller than the pivot is on its left and everything larger is on its right; the pivot is now in its final position. Then sort the two sides recursively. No merging is needed afterwards, everything happens in place, and with a **random** pivot the expected cost is about $1.39\, n\log_2 n$ comparisons, which makes quicksort the fastest general-purpose sort in practice. The catch is that this is an *average*: a pivot that is always the smallest element makes it $\Theta(n^2)$. ::: Merge sort does trivial splitting and careful combining. Quicksort is the mirror image: careful splitting (the partition) and no combining at all. Its whole correctness rests on one fact about the partition: afterwards, the pivot sits at the index it will have in the sorted array, everything left of it is $\le$ it, and everything right of it is $\ge$ it. ```text quicksort(a, lo, hi): # sorts a[lo..hi] if lo < hi: p = partition(a, lo, hi) # pivot lands at its final index p quicksort(a, lo, p - 1) quicksort(a, p + 1, hi) ``` ### Lomuto's partition {#sec-salgo-a4-lomuto} Take the last element as the pivot $x$. When `a[j]` $\le x$, grow the left region by swapping `a[j]` into position $i+1$. It returns $j$ with `a[lo..j]` $\le x \le$ `a[j+1..hi]`. The pivot is not necessarily at $j$; the recursion is on `[lo..j]` and `[j+1..hi]`. Heaps and heapsort {#sec-salgo-a5} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} A **binary max-heap** is an array read as a tree: the children of index $i$ are $2i+1$ and $2i+2$, and every parent is $\ge$ its children, so the root `a[0]` is the maximum. **Sift-down** repairs one out-of-place node in $O(\log n)$ by swapping it with its larger child until it fits. Heapsort builds a heap in $O(n)$, then repeatedly swaps the root (the maximum) to the end of the array and sifts the new root down. That is $O(n \log n)$ in the **worst** case with $O(1)$ extra space, but it is **not stable** and its jumps through memory make it slower than quicksort in practice. ::: Selection sort spends a linear scan to find each maximum (or minimum). Heapsort is selection sort with a better data structure for that one question: the heap answers "what is the largest remaining element?" in $O(1)$ and repairs itself in $O(\log n)$ after the answer is removed. **The array as a tree.** Store a complete binary tree level by level in `a[0..n)`. With 0-based indices the children of $i$ are $2i+1$ and $2i+2$ and the parent of $i > 0$ is $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$; no pointers are stored. The **max-heap property** says `a[parent(i)]` $\ge$ `a[i]` for every $i > 0$. By transitivity the root is the maximum. The tree has height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. (Python's `heapq` and C++'s `priority_queue` are the same structure; `heapq` keeps the *minimum* on top, @sec-lang-p2.) ### Sift-down {#sec-salgo-a5-sift} Suppose both subtrees of node $i$ are heaps but `a[i]` may be smaller than a child. Compare `a[i]` with its children; if the larger child is bigger, swap them and continue from the child's position; stop when `a[i]` is $\ge$ both children or is a leaf. ::: {#fig-salgo-a5-anim} ::: {#df940325 .cell execution_count=15} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}

Otherwise swap with the larger child $c$: now `a[i]` is $\ge$ the other child (the new value is the larger of the two) and $\ge$ the old `a[i]`, so node $i$ is fine; the only possible violation has moved down to $c$. Each step goes one level down, so sift-down costs $O(h)$ for a node of height $h$, at most $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ comparisons. ### Building a heap in linear time {#sec-salgo-a5-build} Leaves are heaps already. Sift down every internal node, from the last one, $\lfloor n/2\rfloor - 1$, back to the root; when node $i$ is processed both its subtrees are heaps, so sift-down's precondition holds. The naive bound is $n/2$ sift-downs of $O(\log n)$ each, but most nodes are near the bottom: at most $\lceil n/2^{h+1}\rceil$ nodes have height $h$, and each costs $O(h)$, so the total is $$ \sum_{h=0}^{\lfloor \log_2 n\rfloor} \left\lceil \frac{n}{2^{h+1}} \right\rceil O(h) = O\!\left(n \sum_{h \ge 0} \frac{h}{2^h}\right) = O(2n) = O(n). $$ In fact the number of swaps is at most the sum of the heights of all nodes, which is less than $n$; the code below asserts it. ### Heapsort {#sec-salgo-a5-sort} ```text heapsort(a): build a max-heap on a[0..n) for end = n-1 down to 1: swap(a[0], a[end]) # the maximum joins the sorted tail sift_down(a, 0, end) # repair the heap a[0..end) ``` **Invariant.** *Before the step with index `end`, `a[0..end]` is a max-heap holding the `end + 1` smallest elements, and `a[end+1..n)` holds the largest elements in sorted order.* The swap moves the maximum of the heap to position `end`, just before the sorted tail and no larger than any tail element, so the tail grows by one and stays sorted; the old last leaf sits at the root and sift-down restores the heap on `a[0..end)`. Stability and the $\Omega(n\log n)$ wall {#sec-salgo-a6} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Two facts close the theory. **Stability** is a property you can test, and you can buy it for any sort by attaching each item's input position to its key. And **no comparison sort can beat $n\log n$**: there are $n!$ possible orders of the input, each comparison has only two outcomes, so some input needs at least $\log_2(n!) \approx n\log_2 n$ comparisons. Merge sort and heapsort meet this bound, so in the comparison model they are optimal up to a constant factor. ::: ### Stability: which sorts have it, and how to buy it {#sec-salgo-a6-stable} Five lessons gave five answers. Insertion sort is stable because it shifts only past *strictly* larger keys (@sec-salgo-a1); merge sort is stable because the merge takes the left head on ties (@sec-salgo-a3). Selection sort, quicksort and heapsort are not, because each makes long-distance swaps that can carry an item over an equal one; the harness found a witness for each. **Buying stability.** Sort the pairs $(\text{key}, \text{input index})$ instead of the keys. Equal keys are then ordered by index, so *every* sort becomes stable, at the price of $O(n)$ extra memory and a slightly more expensive comparison. **Using stability.** To sort records by a primary key and then a secondary key, sort by the *secondary* key first and then *stably* by the primary key: the second pass keeps the secondary order inside each group of equal primary keys. Doing this digit by digit, least significant first, is exactly LSD radix sort (@sec-lts). In one pass, a tuple key `(primary, secondary)` does the same job (@sec-srt-a2). here is the argument for sorting in full (CLRS §8.1). Fix a comparison sort and an input size $n$, and consider inputs that are permutations of $n$ distinct keys. Run the sort and record each comparison it makes and its outcome. Draw the possibilities as a binary tree: each internal node is a comparison "$x_i > x_j$?", its two branches are the two answers, and each leaf is reached when the sort stops and outputs an order. - The tree has **at least $n!$ leaves**: two different input permutations must end at different leaves, because the same sequence of moves cannot sort both. - A binary tree of height $h$ has **at most $2^h$ leaves**. So $2^h \ge n!$, that is $h \ge \log_2(n!)$. The height is the number of comparisons on the worst input, so **every comparison sort makes at least $\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil$ comparisons on some input.** To see how big that is, keep only the largest $n/2$ factors of $n!$, each at least $n/2$: $$ \log_2(n!) \;\ge\; \log_2\!\big((n/2)^{n/2}\big) \;=\; \tfrac{n}{2}\log_2\tfrac{n}{2} \;=\; \Omega(n\log n), $$ {#eq-salgo-lb} and Stirling's formula sharpens it to $\log_2(n!) = n\log_2 n - n\log_2 e + O(\log n) \approx n\log_2 n - 1.44n$. ::: {#fig-salgo-a6-tree} ::: {#64f70b71 .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=19} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](012_sorting_algorithms_files/figure-html/cell-20-output-1.png){width=669 height=271} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](012_sorting_algorithms_files/figure-html/cell-20-output-2.png){width=669 height=271} ::: ::: The decision tree of insertion sort on three items, computed by running it on all $3! = 6$ input orders. There are $6$ leaves, so the height must be at least $\lceil\log_2 6\rceil = 3$, and insertion sort meets it. ::: **The bound also holds on average.** Even if you only care about the average over all $n!$ equally likely inputs, you cannot do better. If the leaves sit at depths $d_1, \dots, d_L$ in a binary tree, then $\sum_\ell 2^{-d_\ell} \le 1$ (Kraft's inequality: each leaf at depth $d$ "uses up" a $2^{-d}$ share of the root). By convexity of $2^{-x}$, $2^{-\bar d} \le \frac1L \sum_\ell 2^{-d_\ell} \le \frac1L$, so the average depth $\bar d \ge \log_2 L \ge \log_2(n!)$. In the figure the average is $8/3 \approx 2.67 \ge \log_2 6 \approx 2.58$. The same argument applies to randomised sorts such as quicksort with random pivots, because fixing the random choices gives an ordinary decision tree (CLRS works this out in an end-of-chapter problem of ch. 8). **What the bound does and does not say.** It is about the *worst* (or average) input in the comparison model, so: - Merge sort ($n\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ comparisons at most) and heapsort ($\le 2n\log_2 n$) are **asymptotically optimal**; nothing in the comparison model is faster than $\Theta(n\log n)$. - An *adaptive* sort may still use $n - 1$ comparisons on a sorted input (insertion sort, Timsort): the bound is about the hardest inputs, not every input. - A sort that reads the keys as numbers is outside the model. Introsort: what `std::sort` runs {#sec-salgo-a7} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Introsort is quicksort with a safety net. It runs ordinary quicksort, but counts how deep the recursion goes. If it ever goes deeper than $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$, the pivots have been bad too often, so it switches to **heapsort** for that part, which guarantees $O(n\log n)$. Small pieces (around 16 elements) are left alone and finished by **one insertion-sort pass** at the end. You get quicksort's speed on typical data and heapsort's worst case on the rest. ::: Quicksort's only weakness is its worst case, and heapsort's only weaknesses are its constant factor and cache behaviour. Musser's **introspective sort** (1997) combines them so that each covers the other. The recursion depth is a cheap, reliable signal: a run of good pivots keeps it near $\log_2 n$; deep recursion means the partitions are unbalanced. ```text introsort(a): loop(a, 0, n, depth = 2 * floor(log2 n)) insertion_sort(a) # one pass over the whole array loop(a, lo, hi, depth): while hi - lo > THRESHOLD: # small blocks are left for the final pass if depth == 0: heapsort(a[lo:hi]); return depth -= 1 pivot = median of a[lo], a[mid], a[hi-1] cut = partition(a, lo, hi, pivot) loop on one side, recurse on the other ``` ::: {#fig-salgo-a7} ::: {#b335748b .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=21} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](012_sorting_algorithms_files/figure-html/cell-22-output-1.png){width=410 height=310} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](012_sorting_algorithms_files/figure-html/cell-22-output-2.png){width=410 height=310} ::: ::: The three parts of introsort. Every block is either partitioned (and the depth budget shrinks), handed to heapsort when the budget is gone, or left as a small unsorted block in its correct position for the final insertion pass. ::: **Why the worst case is $O(n\log n)$.** Every partitioning level costs $O(n)$ in total across the blocks at that depth, and there are at most $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ levels, so partitioning costs $O(n\log n)$. The heapsort calls run on disjoint blocks of total size at most $n$, so they cost $O(n\log n)$ together. After the loop, every element lies in a block of at most $16$ elements that is already in the right position relative to the other blocks, so the final insertion sort makes fewer than $16$ shifts per element, $O(n)$. The final pass is one long insertion sort rather than many small ones because a single tight loop over the array is cheaper in practice. **What the libraries do.** GCC's libstdc++ implements `std::sort` this way: a depth limit of $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$, a median-of-three pivot, a heapsort fallback, and a final insertion sort with a block threshold of 16. Other implementations use the same idea with different details; pattern-defeating quicksort (pdqsort), for example, also recognises already-sorted stretches. Timsort: what Python's `sorted` runs {#sec-salgo-a8} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Real data is rarely random: it often contains stretches that are already in order (a sorted list with a few new items appended, two sorted lists glued together, a reversed block). Timsort finds these **runs**, reverses the descending ones, lengthens short runs to a minimum length with binary insertion sort, and merges neighbouring runs in a balanced order. It is a **stable**, **adaptive** merge sort: $n - 1$ comparisons on sorted input, $O(n\log n)$ in the worst case. ::: Tim Peters wrote Timsort for Python in 2002, and `Objects/listsort.txt` in the CPython source describes it in detail. It is also used for object arrays in Java and for `Array.prototype.sort` in V8 (the JavaScript engine of Chrome and Node.js). Its parts: 1. **Runs.** Scan from the left for the longest prefix that is non-decreasing (`a[0] <= a[1] <= ...`) or *strictly* decreasing (`a[0] > a[1] > ...`). A strictly decreasing run is reversed in place; strictness matters, because reversing a run that contains equal keys would swap their order and break stability. 2. **Minrun.** Very short runs would make many tiny merges, so a run shorter than `minrun` is extended to `minrun` elements (or to the end of the array) with binary insertion sort (@sec-salgo-a1). For $n < 64$, `minrun` $= n$: the whole array is one binary insertion sort. Otherwise `minrun` lies between 32 and 64, chosen so that $n/\text{minrun}$ is a power of two or just below one, which keeps the merges balanced. (The classic rule takes the six leading bits of $n$ and adds 1 if any other bit is set; recent CPython versions refine it so that run lengths differ by at most one.) 3. **The merge stack.** Each new run is pushed on a stack of pending runs, and neighbouring runs are merged until the stack satisfies a balance invariant. In the original design the lengths $A, B, C$ of the three topmost runs must satisfy $A > B + C$ and $B > C$, so lengths grow at least like Fibonacci numbers down the stack and the stack has $O(\log n)$ runs. (In 2015 de Gouw and others found, while trying to verify Java's port formally, that the original check did not always restore the invariant; the fix checks one more level. Current CPython chooses merges with the "powersort" rule of Munro and Wild instead.) Only *neighbouring* runs are ever merged, which is what keeps the sort stable. 4. **Galloping.** When one run keeps winning the merge (seven times in a row at first; the threshold adapts), the merge switches to an exponential search for where the other run's head belongs and copies the whole block at once. Merging a short run into a long one then costs about $O(\text{short} \cdot \log \text{long})$ comparisons instead of $O(\text{short} + \text{long})$. **Cost.** Run detection makes about one comparison per element. On sorted (or strictly decreasing) input there is a single run and no merge, so the sort costs exactly $n - 1$ comparisons. With $\rho$ runs of similar length the merges form a balanced tree of depth $\log_2 \rho$, so the cost is about $n\log_2 \rho$: few runs, nearly linear. On random data all runs are boosted to `minrun` and Timsort behaves like a well-balanced merge sort, $O(n\log n)$ (a 2018 analysis by Auger, Jugé, Nicaud and Pivoteau proved the worst case $O(n\log n)$ for the repaired merge rule). Merges copy the smaller of the two runs into a temporary buffer, so the extra memory is at most $n/2$ elements. | Input | Comparisons | Extra space | |---|---|---| | sorted or strictly decreasing | $n - 1$ | $O(1)$ | | $\rho$ balanced runs | about $n\log_2 \rho$ | $\le n/2$ | | random (worst) | $O(n\log n)$ | $\le n/2$ | **Stable** and **adaptive**; not in place. Every problem has a full statement, a brute-force form and a refined form with matching C++, and stress tests against the brute force; most also have trace boards recorded by *running* the code. ## Pattern 1: Implement a comparison sort from scratch {#sec-salgo-p1} **Where we are.** Part A built the sorts; Part B spends them. P1 is the raw skill: sort *by hand*, with no library call, on an array and then on a linked list, where the lack of random access decides which sort survives. P2 keeps merge sort's split but makes the merge *count* while it sorts. P3 drops the promise to order everything and keeps only quicksort's partition to select one rank. P4 replaces a one-off batch with a stream and keeps only a heap of the $k$ best. P5 stops asking "which order" and asks what the order does with ties. **Recognise it.** "Sort the array **without any built-in sort**, in $O(n\log n)$, with as little extra space as possible"; "sort a **linked list**"; "sort it in place with at most $k$ swaps". These problems *are* the sorting algorithm, so they are the cleanest place to practise A1–A5, their invariants and their edge cases. ::: {.callout-important title="Template"} Pick the sort by the constraint that bites, then prove its invariant. ```text array, O(n log n), stable or simple: merge sort (top-down or bottom-up) O(n) extra array, O(1) extra, worst-case bound: heapsort: build max-heap; swap root to end; sift down linked list: insertion by relinking (O(n^2)), or merge sort by relinking (split with slow/fast pointers; bottom-up for O(1) extra) ``` **Invariant.** Every form keeps "a sorted region that only grows" (prefix for insertion/selection, suffix for heapsort) or "each recursive call returns a sorted permutation of its input" (merge sort). ::: **Complexity.** Insertion and selection $O(n^2)$, merge sort $O(n\log n)$ with $O(n)$ extra on arrays, heapsort $O(n\log n)$ with $O(1)$ extra; on lists, merge sort is $O(n\log n)$ with $O(\log n)$ stack (top-down) or $O(1)$ (bottom-up). ### Problem: Sort an Array {#sec-salgo-p1-a} ::: {.p-statement} Given an integer array `nums` ($1 \le n \le 5 \cdot 10^4$, $-5 \cdot 10^4 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 5 \cdot 10^4$), return it sorted in ascending order. You must **not use any built-in sort**, the time must be $O(n \log n)$, and the extra space should be as small as possible. Duplicates are allowed. Source: [LC 912 · Sort an Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/sort-an-array/){.solved difficulty="Medium"} Example — `nums = [5, 2, 3, 1]`. Output `[1, 2, 3, 5]`. And `[5, 1, 1, 2, 0, 0]` gives `[0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 5]`. ::: ::: {.p-intuition} This is the sorting box itself, not a problem that sorting *helps* with, so the task is to *write* a sort and choose it by the constraints. "$O(n\log n)$" rules out the quadratic sorts; "as little extra space as possible" separates merge sort ($O(n)$ buffer) from heapsort ($O(1)$); and judges for this problem typically include sorted and all-equal arrays, which is exactly where a naive quicksort turns quadratic. ::: ::: {.p-approach} 1. **Selection sort.** At pass $i$ find the minimum of `nums[i..n)` and swap it into position $i$ (@sec-salgo-a2). $O(n^2)$ comparisons, $O(1)$ extra space: too slow here, but the simplest correct sort and the oracle for the other forms. 2. **Merge sort.** Split in half, sort each half, merge the two sorted runs with one shared buffer (@sec-salgo-a3). $\Theta(n\log n)$ on every input and stable, but $O(n)$ extra space. 3. **Heapsort.** Build a max-heap in place, then repeatedly swap the maximum to the end and sift the new root down (@sec-salgo-a5). $O(n\log n)$ in the worst case with $O(1)$ extra space: the form that meets every constraint. **Invariant.** Selection: after pass $i$, `nums[0..i]` is sorted and holds the $i+1$ smallest values. A character $i$ is **weak** if some other character $j$ has *both* $\mathit{attack}_j > \mathit{attack}_i$ **and** $\mathit{defense}_j > \mathit{defense}_i$. Return the number of weak characters. Source: [LC 1996 · The Number of Weak Characters in the Game](https://leetcode.com/problems/the-number-of-weak-characters-in-the-game/){.solved difficulty="Medium"} Example — `[[5,5],[6,3],[3,6]]` → `0`; `[[1,5],[10,4],[4,3]]` → `1` (only $[4,3]$, beaten by $[10,4]$). ::: ::: {.p-intuition} "$j$ dominates $i$ on both axes" is 2-D dominance. Brute force is every pair. The sorting move collapses it to a running maximum: sort by attack ascending and, while sweeping, the question "is there a *strictly larger attack* with larger defense?" becomes "does the maximum defense among strictly-larger-attack characters exceed mine?" — answerable in one right-to-left pass with a single scalar. The entire difficulty lives in **how ties in attack are ordered**, because a same-attack peer must not be allowed to "dominate." ::: ::: {.p-approach} 1. **All-pairs test.** For each $i$, scan for a $j$ beating it on both axes. $O(n^2)$ — the oracle, too slow at $10^5$. 2. **Sort + running-max sweep.** Sort by `(attack ascending, defense descending)`. Sweep right-to-left tracking the maximum defense seen so far. Because equal-attack rows are ordered defense-*descending*, when you are at a row, everything to its right has *strictly greater attack* (never an equal-attack peer), so a right-side defense greater than yours is a genuine dominator. Count it and move on. $O(n \log n)$. **Invariant.** After sorting `(attack ↑, defense ↓)`, at any position the set of rows to the right is exactly the rows with strictly greater attack **or** equal attack and $\le$ defense; the defense-descending tie-break removes the equal-attack rows from ever being counted as dominators, so `max_defense_right > my_defense` iff a true dominator exists. ::: The buttons are in order. Sweep right-to-left holding `best` = the maximum defense seen so far (which all belong to strictly-greater-attack characters, thanks to the tie-break). Insertion and selection sort grow a sorted prefix one element at a time and pay $O(n^2)$ for it (A1, A2). Merge sort replaces "one element at a time" with "two sorted halves at a time", which is balanced by construction and gives $\Theta(n\log n)$ always, plus a merge that can count (A3, P1, P2). Quicksort does the work before recursing instead of after, and its partition, applied to one side only, selects a rank in expected linear time (A4, P3). Heapsort keeps selection sort's idea but answers "what is the maximum?" with a heap, which also powers top-$k$ and streams (A5, P4). The decision tree shows that $n\log n$ comparisons cannot be beaten (A6), so the libraries compete on everything else: introsort on the worst case, Timsort on existing order and stability (A7, A8), and stability itself becomes a tool (P5). Shift only while strictly greater (@sec-salgo-a1). - **A strict `<` for the left head in a merge.** Taking the right head on ties (`L[i] < R[j]` for the left) makes merge sort unstable. Take the left head when `L[i] <= R[j]` (@sec-salgo-a3). - **A fixed pivot on sorted input.** Always choosing `a[hi]` (or `a[lo]`) splits sorted data $0 \mid n-1$ and runs in $\Theta(n^2)$, with $\Theta(n)$ recursion depth. Randomise the pivot or use median-of-three, and recurse into the smaller side (@sec-salgo-a4). - **Lomuto's partition on many equal keys.** Every element is $\le$ the pivot, so the split is $n-1 \mid 0$ again. Use Hoare's partition, which stops on equal keys, or the three-way partition (@sec-salgo-a4-hoare). - **Hoare's partition with the pivot at `a[hi]`.** With the classic code the returned $j$ can equal `hi`, so the recursion on `[lo..j]` never shrinks. Take the pivot from the middle (or the front), as in @sec-salgo-a4-hoare. - **Off-by-one in heap indices.** With 0-based arrays the children of $i$ are $2i+1$ and $2i+2$ and the last internal node is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor - 1$; the 1-based formulas $2i, 2i+1$ silently skip or duplicate nodes (@sec-salgo-a5). - **Building a heap with $n$ pushes and calling it $O(n)$.** Repeated `push` is $O(n\log n)$; bottom-up sift-down (`heapify`, `make_heap`) is $O(n)$ (@sec-salgo-a5-build). - **Assuming `std::sort` is stable.** It is introsort and is not stable; use `std::stable_sort`, or a tuple key, when input order inside ties matters (@sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-p5-a). - **Reversing a non-strictly descending run.** A run like $5, 3, 3, 1$ reversed in place swaps the two $3$s; Timsort only reverses *strictly* descending runs (@sec-salgo-a8). - **Counting crossings with a nested loop.** Once both halves are sorted, the cross count is one forward pointer; re-scanning is the $O(n^2)$ you came to avoid (@sec-salgo-p2-a, @sec-salgo-p2-c). - **`2 * nums[j]` in 32-bit.** For values near $2^{31}$ the doubling overflows; widen to `long long` first (@sec-salgo-p2-c). - **Sorting a linked list with quicksort or heapsort.** No random access means no index-based partition and no `2i+1` children; use merge sort by relinking (@sec-salgo-p1-c). - **Re-sorting the whole pool per stream query.** That makes each `add` $O(n\log n)$; a size-$k$ heap makes it $O(\log k)$ (@sec-salgo-p4-b). - **Wrong tie-break direction on dominance.** Sorting `(attack, defense)` both ascending lets an equal-attack character "dominate" its peer; `(attack ASC, defense DESC)` is what makes the right-to-left sweep correct (@sec-salgo-p5-b). ::: ## Exercises **1. If the test were `>=`, an element equal to `key` would also be shifted, so `key` would land *before* an equal element that came first in the input, breaking input order. [E] Bubble sort repeatedly sweeps the array and swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs. A binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$ leaves, so $2^h \ge n!$ and the worst case $h \ge \log_2(n!)$. For the estimate, $n! \ge n(n-1)\cdots(\lceil n/2\rceil) \ge (n/2)^{n/2}$, so $\log_2(n!) \ge \tfrac n2\log_2\tfrac n2$. [M] Compute Timsort's classic `minrun` for $n = 63$, $n = 1000$ and $n = 2112$, and explain why `minrun` is chosen so that $n / \text{minrun}$ is close to a power of two.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} $n = 63 < 64$: `minrun` $= 63$, a single binary insertion sort. $n = 1000 = 1111101000_2$: the top six bits are $111110_2 = 62$, and a lower bit is set, so `minrun` $= 63$ (giving 16 runs of about 63). $n = 2112 = 100001000000_2$: top six bits $100001_2 = 33$, no lower bit set, so `minrun` $= 33$ and $2112 = 64 \cdot 33$ splits into exactly 64 runs. [M] In @sec-salgo-p2-b the answer credits a left element with `j`, the number of right-half elements already merged. Name five comparison sorts and give each one's time, extra space and stability.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Insertion: $O(n^2)$ worst, $O(n)$ best, $O(1)$ space, stable. Selection: $\Theta(n^2)$ always, $O(1)$, not stable. Merge sort: $\Theta(n\log n)$ always, $O(n)$, stable. Quicksort: $O(n\log n)$ expected, $O(n^2)$ worst, $O(\log n)$ stack, not stable. Heapsort: $O(n\log n)$ worst, $O(1)$, not stable (@sec-salgo-a9). ::: **2. Why is quicksort $O(n^2)$ on sorted input with a last-element pivot, and what are the standard fixes?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} The last element of a sorted range is its maximum, so every partition splits $n-1 \mid 0$ and the costs add up to $\binom n2$. Fixes: a random pivot (expected $O(n\log n)$ on every input), median-of-three, and introsort's heapsort fallback after a depth limit (a guarantee). Separately, a three-way or Hoare partition fixes the all-equal-keys blow-up (@sec-salgo-a4-analysis, @sec-salgo-a7). ::: **3. What makes merge sort $\Theta(n\log n)$ in the worst case while quicksort is only $O(n\log n)$ on average?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Merge sort's split is input-independent (always the middle), so its recursion tree always has $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$ levels of $O(n)$ work. Quicksort's split depends on the pivot's rank, which can be extreme again and again, giving $n$ levels. Balanced by construction versus balanced by luck (@sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-a4). ::: **4. Why is quicksort usually faster than merge sort and heapsort in practice, even though all three are $O(n\log n)$?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Its inner loop is a sequential scan that compares with one pivot held in a register and moves few elements; it works in place, so it touches less memory and uses the cache well. Merge sort moves every element at every level and needs a buffer; heapsort jumps between $i$ and $2i+1$, which is cache-unfriendly, and makes about twice as many comparisons. The expected $1.39\,n\log_2 n$ comparisons of random-pivot quicksort are a small price for that (@sec-salgo-a4-analysis, @sec-salgo-a5). ::: **5. How do you keep quicksort's stack depth $O(\log n)$ even in its worst case?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Recurse into the smaller side and loop (tail-iterate) on the larger side. The smaller side has at most half the elements, so each nested call at least halves the size and the depth is at most $\log_2 n$; time can still be quadratic, but the stack cannot overflow (@sec-salgo-a4-analysis). ::: **6. State the $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound and its hypothesis. How do counting and radix sort escape it?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Any comparison sort makes at least $\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil = \Theta(n\log n)$ comparisons in the worst case (and on average): its decision tree needs $n!$ leaves and a binary tree of height $h$ has at most $2^h$. The hypothesis is that the algorithm learns about keys only through pairwise comparisons. Counting and radix sort use key values as array indices, which is not a comparison, so they can run in $O(n + k)$ (@sec-salgo-a6-bound, @sec-lts). ::: **7. Why is building a heap $O(n)$ and not $O(n\log n)$?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Bottom-up building sifts each node down at most its height, and most nodes are near the bottom: about $n/2$ leaves cost nothing, $n/4$ nodes cost one level, $n/8$ cost two, and so on. The sum $\sum_h \frac{n}{2^{h+1}} h$ is less than $n$. Only repeated pushes (sift-up from the bottom for each new element) cost $O(n\log n)$ (@sec-salgo-a5-build). ::: **8. What is a stable sort, why does it matter, and which standard sorts are stable?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Stability keeps equal-key items in input order. It matters for multi-key sorting by successive passes, for keeping a group in its original order (LC 937's digit-logs), and for predictable output. Python's `sorted` and `list.sort` (Timsort) and C++ `std::stable_sort` are stable; C++ `std::sort` is not. Any sort becomes stable if it sorts `(key, index)` pairs (@sec-salgo-a6-stable, @sec-salgo-p5-a). ::: **9. What do `std::sort` and Python's `sorted` actually run?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} `std::sort` (in GCC's libstdc++) is introsort: median-of-three quicksort with a recursion depth limit of $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$, a heapsort fallback when the limit is hit, and a final insertion sort over blocks of at most 16; worst case $O(n\log n)$, not stable. `sorted` is Timsort: natural runs (strictly descending ones reversed), short runs extended to `minrun` by binary insertion sort, a stack of runs merged with a balance rule, galloping merges; stable, $n - 1$ comparisons on sorted input, $O(n\log n)$ worst case (@sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-a8). ::: **10. How do you count inversions in $O(n\log n)$?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Merge sort with a counter. Pairs within a half are counted recursively; for the pairs across the halves, when a right-half element is output before the left-half elements still waiting, it forms an inversion with each of them, so add their number. Both halves are sorted, so this is linear per merge. Sort indices instead of values to get per-element counts (@sec-salgo-p2-a, @sec-salgo-p2-b). ::: **11. Find the $k$-th largest element without sorting. Give the algorithm, its cost and the alternative for a stream.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Quickselect: partition around a random pivot and continue only into the side that contains index $n - k$; expected $O(n)$, in place, worst case $O(n^2)$ (median of medians or introselect make it linear in the worst case). Why is merge sort, not quicksort or heapsort, the sort for a linked list?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} A list has no random access: heapsort's children $2i+1, 2i+2$ cannot be reached cheaply, and quicksort's partition swaps elements at arbitrary positions. Merge sort splits with a slow/fast walk and merges by relinking `next` pointers, with no copying; done bottom-up it needs only $O(1)$ extra memory (@sec-salgo-p1-c). ::: **13. When do you keep a heap instead of sorting?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} When you need the extreme, or the $k$ extremes, repeatedly but never the full order: top-$k$ ($O(n\log k)$ instead of $O(n\log n)$), running medians, priority scheduling, $k$-way merging, and anything streaming. Extracting *all* $n$ elements from a heap is heapsort, $O(n\log n)$, so the win comes only from extracting or keeping far fewer than $n$ (@sec-salgo-a5, @sec-salgo-p4). ::: **14. How would you sort 100 GB of records on a machine with 8 GB of memory?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} External merge sort. Pass 1: read the file in chunks that fit in memory, sort each chunk (any in-memory sort), write it out as a sorted run: about 13 runs. Pass 2: merge all runs at once with a min-heap holding the current head of each run, reading and writing sequentially with large buffers. If there are too many runs for one pass, merge them in groups. Merge sort fits because the merge reads its inputs strictly in order (@sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-p4). ::: **15. Insertion sort is $O(n^2)$. Why do production sorts still use it?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Its cost is $O(n + \text{inversions})$ with a tiny constant: for blocks of a few dozen elements, or data that is nearly sorted, it beats the $n\log n$ sorts and their overhead. Introsort finishes blocks of at most 16 with one insertion pass, and Timsort extends short runs with binary insertion sort, which needs only $O(\log n)$ comparisons per element (@sec-salgo-a1, @sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-a8). ::: **16. How does selection sort differ from insertion sort in what it minimises?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Insertion sort minimises work on nearly sorted input: $O(n + \text{inversions})$ comparisons and moves. Selection sort always makes $\binom n2$ comparisons but at most $n - 1$ swaps, so it minimises writes, which matters when moving an element is expensive (@sec-salgo-a1, @sec-salgo-a2). ::: **17. For "count pairs with $a_i > 2a_j$, $i < j$", give the brute force, the faster method and the subtle bug.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Brute force: test all pairs, $O(n^2)$. Faster: merge sort with a separate cross-count pass before each merge; both halves are sorted, so one forward pointer counts the pairs in $O(n)$ per level, $O(n\log n)$ in total. Bug: `2 * a[j]` overflows 32-bit integers for values near $2^{31}$; use 64-bit (@sec-salgo-p2-c). ::: **18. Why does Timsort make only $n - 1$ comparisons on an already sorted list, and does that contradict the lower bound?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Run detection compares each element with its predecessor once; on sorted input that finds a single run of length $n$ with $n - 1$ comparisons, and there is nothing to merge. It does not contradict the lower bound, which is about the *worst* (or average) input: an adaptive sort may be fast on easy inputs as long as some inputs still cost $\Omega(n\log n)$ (@sec-salgo-a8, @sec-salgo-a6-bound). ::: ## Summary ::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"} - **Insertion** `while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: a[j+1] = a[j]; j -= 1`; $O(n + \text{inversions})$, in place, stable (@sec-salgo-a1). - **Selection** `swap(a[i], a[argmin a[i..]])`; $\binom n2$ comparisons, $\le n-1$ swaps, not stable (@sec-salgo-a2). - **Merge** sort the halves, merge taking the left head on ties (`L[i] <= R[j]`); $\Theta(n\log n)$ always, $O(n)$ extra, stable; bottom-up needs no recursion (@sec-salgo-a3). - **Quicksort** random pivot; Lomuto (`a[j] <= x` grows the left region), Hoare (two fingers, middle pivot), or three-way `< == >`; expected $2n\ln n$ comparisons; recurse on the smaller side (@sec-salgo-a4). - **Quickselect** partition, keep only the side with index $t$; expected $O(n)$ (@sec-salgo-a4-select). - **Heap** children $2i+1, 2i+2$; sift-down swaps with the larger child; build bottom-up in $O(n)$; heapsort swaps the root to the end, $O(n\log n)$, $O(1)$ extra, not stable (@sec-salgo-a5). - **Lower bound** $\lceil\log_2(n!)\rceil \ge \tfrac n2\log_2\tfrac n2$ comparisons, worst case and average (@sec-salgo-a6-bound). - **Libraries** introsort = quicksort + depth limit $2\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor$ + heapsort + final insertion; Timsort = runs + minrun + merge stack + galloping, stable (@sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-a8). - **Patterns** count across the merge (P2), select one rank (P3), bounded heap (P4), stable sort or designed tie-break (P5). ::: - Every sort here keeps an invariant about a region that only grows: a sorted prefix, a sorted suffix, or "each call returns a sorted permutation" (@sec-salgo-a1, @sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-a5). - Insertion sort's cost is the number of inversions plus $n$; that makes it the best sort for tiny and nearly sorted inputs and the finisher inside hybrids (@sec-salgo-a1). - Merge sort is balanced by construction: $\Theta(n\log n)$ always, stable, and its merge streams, counts crossings and relinks lists (@sec-salgo-a3, @sec-salgo-p1-c, @sec-salgo-p2). - Quicksort is balanced on average: with a random pivot every input costs about $1.39\,n\log_2 n$ comparisons; three-way partitioning handles duplicates and one-sided recursion selects a rank in expected $O(n)$ (@sec-salgo-a4, @sec-salgo-p3-a). - Heapsort is selection sort with a heap: $O(n\log n)$ worst case in $O(1)$ memory; the bounded heap is the top-$k$ and streaming workhorse (@sec-salgo-a5, @sec-salgo-p4). - No comparison sort beats $\log_2(n!)$ comparisons on its worst or average input; adaptive sorts are fast on easy inputs without contradicting this (@sec-salgo-a6-bound). - Library sorts are hybrids: introsort guarantees the worst case, Timsort exploits runs and is stable; know which one your language runs (@sec-salgo-a7, @sec-salgo-a8). - Stability and tie-break direction are design decisions, not details; they decide whole problems (@sec-salgo-p5). ## Practice ladder Ordered by concept, following the chapter.
